endangered-species-s1.title: Traits that raise extinction risk, and protections

endangered-species-s2.title: How the bald eagle came back
endangered-species-s2.passage: In 1963 only 417 nesting pairs of bald eagles were left in the lower 48 states. The pesticide DDT, sprayed widely after World War II, washed into lakes and built up in the fish that eagles eat. In the eagles it caused thin eggshells that broke during nesting. The United States banned DDT for most uses in 1972, and the Endangered Species Act protected the birds and their nesting sites from shooting and disturbance. By 2007 there were 9,789 nesting pairs, and the bald eagle was removed from the endangered and threatened species list.
endangered-species-s2.source: Summarized from U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service reports on bald eagle recovery (2007).

items.q: Under the Endangered Species Act, what is the difference between an endangered and a threatened species?
options: Endangered: at risk now; threatened: soon
Endangered lives in the US; threatened lives overseas
Threatened is closer to extinction than endangered
Endangered refers to plants, and threatened to animals

why.correct: Endangered: in danger of extinction throughout all or a significant part of its range. Threatened: likely to become endangered in the foreseeable future.
options: Right: endangered is in danger of extinction in all or much of its range; threatened is likely to become endangered.
Both categories are about extinction risk, not location.
It is the other way around: endangered is the more serious category.
Both categories apply to plants and animals.

items.q: Which species is most at risk of extinction?
options: A fast-breeding generalist found on most continents
A slow-breeding specialist with a small range
A common bird that eats many kinds of seeds
A weed that spreads easily into disturbed land

why.correct: Extinction risk rises with specialization, slow reproduction, small or isolated populations and large territory needs.
options: Generalists with many offspring and wide ranges are least at risk.
Right: specialist and K-selected traits plus a small range make recovery hard.
A broad diet and large numbers lower risk.
Weedy, r-selected species thrive in disturbed land.
It sets limits on CO₂ emissions
It phases out ozone-depleting chemicals
It limits trade in protected species
It protects wetlands used by migrating birds

why.correct: CITES (the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species) regulates trade in species such as elephants (ivory), rhinos and many orchids.
options: That is a climate agreement, not CITES.
That is the Montreal Protocol.
Right: CITES is a treaty that bans or limits trade in endangered plants and animals and their parts.
That describes a wetland treaty, not CITES.

items.q: According to the figure, which trait raises extinction risk?
options: A broad diet
A large population
High genetic diversity
Slow reproduction

why.correct: Slow reproduction, narrow niches, small populations, large territories, low genetic diversity and hunting all raise risk.
options: A broad diet lowers risk; the figure lists a narrow diet.
Small or isolated populations are at risk.
The figure lists low genetic diversity as a risk.
Right: K-selected species replace losses slowly.

items.q: Giant pandas eat mostly bamboo, have one cub every two or three years, and live in a few mountain forests. Using the figure, how many risk traits do these facts show?
options: Three
One
Five
Zero

why.correct: Specialist diet + K-selected reproduction + small, fragmented range.
options: Right: a narrow diet, slow reproduction and a small, isolated range.
Each fact shows a different risk trait.
The facts show three of the figure’s traits.
All three facts match traits in the figure.

items.q: Which protection in the figure best addresses rhinos killed for their horns to be sold abroad?
options: Captive breeding
CITES
The Endangered Species Act
A national park

why.correct: Match the protection to the threat: international trade calls for an international treaty.
options: Breeding adds animals but does not stop the trade that kills them.
Right: it controls the international trade that drives the poaching.
The ESA is a US law; the trade crosses many countries.
A park protects land, but horns are sold across borders; the threat here is trade.

items.q: What is the main claim of the passage?
options: Bald eagles were not really at risk
Captive breeding alone saved the bald eagle
A DDT ban and protection let eagles recover
Hunting is now the main threat to bald eagles

why.correct: The author links the recovery to two actions: banning DDT and protecting the birds and their nests.
options: The passage describes a fall to 417 nesting pairs.
The passage credits the DDT ban and protection, not breeding alone.
Right: the passage credits the DDT ban and legal protection.
The passage says shooting was banned.

items.q: Using the passage, what was the percent change in nesting pairs from 1963 to 2007?

mistakes.why: You divided by the new value. Use (new − old) ÷ old × 100: (9,789 − 417) ÷ 417 × 100.
That is how many times larger the population became (about 23.5). Percent change is (new − old) ÷ old × 100.

items.q: Which actions helped the bald eagle recover? Choose the best answer.
options: A DDT ban plus legal protection
Moving most eagles into zoos
Introducing eagles from Europe
Spraying more pesticides on lakes

why.correct: DDT biomagnified up food chains and thinned eggshells; banning it removed the cause.
options: Right: DDT thinned eggshells; the 1972 ban and ESA protection let numbers recover.
Most eagles stayed wild; captive breeding played a small part.
Bald eagles are North American; none were brought from Europe.
Pesticides such as DDT caused the decline.

items.q: A wildlife refuge counts 240 adult whooping cranes. Each year, 6% of adults die and new adults join equal to 9% of the count. Write the setup for the change in adults after one year, then the answer.

mistakes.why: Gains minus losses: new adults (9%) minus deaths (6%). This order gives a negative number.
The rates are percents: use 0.09 and 0.06, or divide by 100.
You used 3 instead of 3%. Net growth is 3% of 240: 240 × 0.03 = 7.2, about 7 adults.

items.q: Which actions protect endangered species? Select all that apply.
options: Protecting critical habitat from development
Captive breeding and reintroduction
Increasing the trade in rare animal parts
Clearing forest for new housing

why.correct: Protect habitat, control trade and hunting, and breed and reintroduce where numbers are very low.
options: Right: losing habitat is the main threat to most listed species.
Right: used for California condors and black-footed ferrets.
Trade drives poaching; CITES restricts it.
Clearing habitat raises extinction risk.

items.q: Why is low genetic diversity dangerous for a small population of an endangered species?
options: It makes individuals live much longer
It makes the population grow too fast
It means the species becomes invasive
It cannot adapt well to disease or change

why.correct: A population bottleneck removes variation, leaving less raw material for adaptation and more inbreeding.
options: Low diversity does not lengthen life.
Small, inbred populations tend to grow slowly.
Invasive species are usually common and widespread.
Right: with few gene variants, a disease or change can hit nearly every individual.

items.q: A rare salamander lives in a few streams in one forest that a company plans to log. Propose a solution that protects the salamander and say how it works.

why.correct: Fit the solution to the threat (logging of a small habitat) and say how it works.

solution.label: Solution
options: the Endangered Species Act
more logging roads
pesticide spraying

why.1: Roads fragment habitat and add runoff.

action.label: Action
options: listing the salamander and protecting its streams as critical habitat
moving it to a zoo for good
logging the forest faster

why.1: Keeping it in a zoo forever does not protect the wild population.
why.2: Faster logging removes the habitat sooner.

effect.label: How it works
options: bans logging that would destroy the streams it needs
raises the price of lumber
adds nutrients to the streams

why.1: Price changes do not protect a specific habitat.
why.2: Extra nutrients would harm the streams.

specific.model: Use the Endangered Species Act by listing the salamander and protecting its streams as critical habitat, because it bans logging that would destroy the streams, so the population keeps the shaded, cool water it needs to survive and breed.

items.q: Which is a common criticism of the Endangered Species Act?
options: It protects plants, which have no economic value
It can limit how owners use land
It allows unlimited hunting of listed species
It applies to fish but not to birds

why.correct: The ESA weighs conservation against land use; debates often center on private land and jobs.
options: Plants provide food, medicine and ecosystem services.
Right: protecting critical habitat can restrict logging, building or farming.
It bans harming listed species.
It applies to all kinds of plants and animals.

items.q: Why do species with large territories, such as wolves and tigers, face high extinction risk?
options: They reproduce faster than they can find food
They are generalists that compete with people
They need more land than is left whole
They have no predators of their own

why.correct: Large-territory species collide with people when habitat is cut into pieces too small to support them.
options: These predators reproduce slowly.
The key issue is the amount of space they need.
Right: as habitat shrinks and fragments, few areas are large enough.
Lacking predators does not raise extinction risk.
